title: Edible sugar lace panels
subtitle: applying ready-made sugar lace sheets to cakes
excerpt: Edible sugar lace is a thin, flexible sheet produced from a silicone lace mould and a starch-based lace mixture. Once dry, it peels away from the mould like a fragile fabric and adheres directly to a smooth buttercream or fondant surface. It is the most efficient way to achieve a lace-pattern exterior on a wedding or celebration cake without hand-piping hundreds of individual stitches.
sourceNotes: Edible sugar lace products and moulds for home decorators emerged in the early 2010s, led by commercial products like 'Sugarveil' and 'SK Sugar Florist Paste' lace mixes. Before these products, lace patterns on cakes were achieved with royal icing run-out techniques, brush embroidery, or overpiped net patterns, all significantly more labour-intensive. The silicone lace mould technique is now standard in wedding cake decorating. The sheets behave like a very thin, flexible fondant once dry, they tear easily but adhere strongly to slightly tacky buttercream or lightly moistened fondant.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The lace sheets can be dried and stored flat between sheets of parchment for up to a week before use.

content.text: Edible sugar lace panels give a delicate lace texture to the sides of a cake without hand-piping. The process has three stages: fill the mould, dry the sheet, and apply it to the cake. The lace is fragile until it's on the cake, so handle it with care. It works best on a cold, smooth base, chilled buttercream or fondant, where it adheres on contact.

content.text: Mix the lace powder with water according to the packet instructions. The consistency should be like thin, pourable custard. Spoon the mixture over the silicone lace mould and spread it with a palette knife or bank card, pressing into all the recesses and scraping away every trace of paste from the raised sections of the pattern. Any residue on the raised parts will leave a film over the lace design once dry.

Leave the mould flat at room temperature for 3 to 4 hours until the lace is completely dry and no longer tacky. The surface should be matte. Do not try to peel it before it's dry, the sheet will tear at every junction in the lace pattern. To speed this up, place the mould in an oven set to 80°C for 30 minutes, then cool completely before peeling.
Peel and apply to the cake

Peel a corner of the lace gently from the mould, working slowly across the sheet. Roll the sheet loosely rather than folding it, folds crack the lace. Hold one end against the side of the cake and unroll it along the surface, pressing lightly to adhere. The lace sticks to slightly tacky chilled buttercream without any adhesive; for fondant-covered cakes, brush a thin layer of water or clear alcohol over the surface first. Trim any overlap with a sharp knife or scissors at the join line.

If the panel tears when you peel it away, it needs more drying time. Return it to a very low oven (60°C) for another 5 minutes and try again. Avoid working in a humid kitchen; lace dries poorly above 70% humidity. If the mix pours too thickly and buries the mould detail, add a teaspoon of water at a time and stir gently until the batter flows level. Take care not to spread the mix beyond the mould edges or the overhang will tear. If the finished panel looks dull rather than glossy, do not panic: a light brush of edible pearl lustre mixed with clear spirit restores the sheen instantly.
